newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH MONEY RATES RISE SEEN AS TEMPORARY.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH MONEY RATES RISE SEEN AS TEMPORARY.

text.p: Dutch money rates moved up slightly on Tuesday, but dealers said the rise was only temporary as the current allocation kept call money rates at a high level and the end-of-year effect was pushing deposits a little higher.
"Rates will nudge down again," said one dealer. He said the idea that rates had seen the bottom was currently fading.
"The current bump is temporary and I can see money rates edging down again at the start of 1997," said another dealer.
"It won't be much, but there is still some space for lower rates," he said.
Call money was bid between 2.75-81 percent, which is well above the special advances rate of 2.50 percent.
The special advances is a short-term loan offered to commercial banks at a rate fixed by the central bank.
The duration differs, but is usually around four days.

The current six-day advances pact of 3.74 billion guilders expires on Thursday and dealers said the rate for call money could ease after the central bank allocates liquidity under the new pact. "The current pact is quite tight," said one dealer.
One-month deposits added two basis points to 2.84 percent bid and six-month paper rose two basis points to 3.04 percent.
The guilder lost some ground versus the mark at 112.1850 per 100 marks from 112.1725 on Monday.
The Dutch Finance Ministry Agent said earlier today it did not raise any liquidity through its Dutch Treasury Certificate programmes during the last week.
The Agency updates the survey on the amount of DTCs every Tuesday.
"It does not look like the government wants to raise more liquidity through its DTC programmes," said one dealer.
